children: CoreWeave
is looking to tap the massive pools of capital managed by insurance companies as it searches for cheaper, longer-term financing to fund its rapidly expanding AI infrastructure build-out.
According to the Financial Times, co-founder Brannin McBee wants CoreWeave to secure
investment-grade ratings for more of its chip-backed debt and eventually for the company itself
, opening the door to a much broader universe of institutional investors.
It's unlimited. Like, that's all the money in the world that sits in the insurance tranche, McBee said.
The financing push comes after an extraordinary year of capital raising.
CoreWeave has raised more than
$35 billion in 2026
through chip-backed loans, high-yield bonds, convertible debt and equity sales. Its debt and lease obligations stood at roughly
$52 billion at the end of June
One important precedent is already in place.
An
$8.5 billion loan

backed by computing infrastructure and a contract with Meta Platforms received an investment-grade rating. CoreWeave now wants to extend that model to debt backed by contracts with lower-rated AI labs.
That could matter significantly because insurance companies typically prefer investment-grade assets, and gaining access to that capital could reduce CoreWeave's reliance on higher-cost financing.
The demand side remains strong.
McBee said nearly all of CoreWeave's
2027 capacity has already been sold
, while the company has also signed contracts extending into 2028 and beyond.
Investor Takeaway
I think the key issue here is no longer whether CoreWeave can find AI demand.
It is whether it can
finance that demand cheaply enough
The company has enormous contracted capacity, but it also carries a very large debt and lease burden. That makes the cost and structure of capital almost as important as revenue growth.
Winning investment-grade ratings on more asset-backed debt could materially improve that equation by bringing in insurers and other lower-cost institutional capital.
For investors, the key things to watch are
credit ratings, interest expense, refinancing costs, debt-to-cash-flow trends and how much of future capacity is backed by long-term contracts with high-quality customers

If CoreWeave can keep pre-selling capacity while lowering its financing costs, the business model becomes much more durable. If not, the scale of its debt burden could become increasingly difficult to ignore.

title: CoreWeave's Next Big Move Could Reshape its AI Ambitions
